entries.title: Rome's Colosseum closes after worker falls to his death
entries.summary: The man had been working on a new lighting installation in the iconic Roman amphitheater. Italian authorities said they were working on determining the circumstances of the accident.
entries.content:
Italy

Rome's Colosseum closes after worker falls to his death

September 23, 2026

The man had been working on a new lighting installation in the iconic Roman amphitheater. Italian authorities said they were working on determining the circumstances of the accident.

The Colosseum in Rome was closed on Wednesday after a worker fell to his death overnight.

Andrea Moretti, 22, died after falling while working on a new lighting installation.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she hoped that the cause of the accident would be clarified as soon as possible.

"We are deeply shocked and saddened by the news of the tragic death of Andrea Moretti, a skilled worker who lost his life last night following an accident at the Colosseum," she said. "For a person to die at the age of 22 is unacceptable and even more so when it happens in the workplace."

Italian Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli described the incident as a "tragic event that has left us shocked and stunned."

The Culture Ministry said "the second-tier section where the accident occurred" would be closed

Authorities were working on determining the circumstances of the accident, according to the statement.

The ministry said the site would be fully closed to the public for the day after all visitors leave.

The part of the site where the accident occurred had already been closed early on Wednesday.

What is Rome's Colosseum?

The ancient Colosseum is the world's largest amphitheater.

It was built in the first century under the Roman Empire. It was used to host gladiator fights, executions and animal hunts.

It is one of Rome's most iconic sites and gets up to 20,000 visitors a day at peak times.

entries.title: OECD says growth 'resilient' in 2026 despite Middle East war
entries.summary: The OECD group of industrialized nations put its 2026 growth forecast at 2.9%. It said investment in AI was helping drive growth, while the war in the Middle East was fueling inflation.
entries.content:
BusinessGlobal issues

Growth 'resilient' despite Middle East war, OECD says

September 23, 2026

The OECD group of industrialized nations put its 2026 growth forecast at 2.9%. It said investment in AI was helping drive growth, while the war in the Middle East was fueling inflation.

The OECD group of industrialized countries on Wednesday lifted its global growth forecast for 2026 despite the war in the Middle East.

It put the figure at 2.9%, an increase of 0.1 percentage points over June's estimates.

The 38-member Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) is a Paris-based forum for industrialized nations.

What did the OECD say about 2026 growth?

The OECD said growth remained "resilient" in 2026, and that "broader financial conditions remain supportive."

It added that the impact of the Middle East war was being softened by other factors.

"Sizeable oil inventories, additional supply from outside the Gulf economies and discretionary government support measures all helped to cushion the impact on the global economy," the group said.

It said investments in artificial intelligence could result in "stronger growth than projected," but warned that growth could still slow if investments do not pay off as expected.

Growth still threatened

However, global growth has dropped from last year's 3.4%, and the OECD has also dropped its 2027 forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3%.

Governments around the world have begun raising interest rates to cushion inflationary pressures sparked by rising oil and gas prices.

The OECD stressed that the outlook depends on whether a lasting resolution to the conflict is found, as continued fighting would likely lead to higher inflation.

The crisis has also led to an increase in government bond yields.

"Rising bond yields underline more than ever the need for enhanced efforts to contain and reallocate government spending, improve public-sector efficiency and strengthen revenues to ensure longer-term debt sustainability and maintain the ability of governments to react to significant shocks," the OECD said.

It said that other threats include weather-related risks like the El Nino pattern, which could cause supply bottlenecks and high food costs.

entries.title: Campus Project 2026: Georgia Takes Center Stage
entries.summary: The Beethovenfest exchange project brings German and Georgian musical traditions together. And the reasons go beyond music.
entries.content:
September 23, 2026

The Beethovenfest exchange project brings German and Georgian musical traditions together. And the reasons go beyond music.

Last June, a group of around 20 young German musicians — members of the Federal Youth Orchestra and Federal Youth Choir — arrived in Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia. They were immediately captivated by the Caucasus metropolis and its overwhelming atmosphere of relaxed freedom.

But that freedom can be deceptive. Everyone was aware of Georgia's tense political and social situation and had seen images of the pro-European protests in Tbilisi.

The next morning, the German musicians gathered in a simple room in central Tbilisi with an equally sized group of young Georgian musicians from the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra as well as singers from the independent music scene.

Finding a Shared Sound

The young musicians from Georgia and members of the Federal Youth Orchestra first met in June in Tbilisi to rehearse for the joint "Campus Concert" at the Beethovenfest in Bonn.

But before that, they had to find a shared sound and develop a program that would bring together two major musical traditions from the two countries.

"We Georgians are known as hot-blooded Southerners with a lot of raw emotion," says Mirian Kokhunaishvili, conductor and artistic director of the project. "Sometimes the intensity of our emotions is higher than in German music. But once you listen to German music, you understand that people are full of emotions there, too, but there's different approaches to how we express them. In music, I couldn't see any differences."

After final rehearsals in Bonn, joint concerts will take place on Sept. 23 and 24: first at the Beethovenfest in Bonn and the following day in Berlin. DW will broadcast the concert live on the DW Classical Music YouTube channel.

A Political Message Behind the Music

The Campus project is about more than an exciting musical experiment — and not just for the Georgian participants.

"One goal is to bring the classical repertoire of Georgian music closer to an international audience," says Mirian Kokhunaishvili. "And then we want to send a message. We couldn't simply play and sing without reflecting the reality around us."

For Kokhunaishvili, the music itself is the strongest message: "Our concert is about the geopolitical reality we live in. We want to express our hope for Europe — not just the hope of joining something somewhere, but that this is our shared home. We are fighting to belong there. The core message is that in Georgia, we share Western European values of human rights."

A highlight of the program is a new synthesis arranged by Georgian composer Mika Mdinaradze. The composition combines Beethoven's choral piece "Europa steht!" ("Europe Stands!") from the cantata "The Glorious Moment" with traditional Georgian songs.

"Beethoven naturally remains unmistakable, while the Georgian polyphonic structures preserve their own identity," Mdinaradze explains in an interview with DW. "Together, they create a sonic model of Europe — a dialogue instead of forced unity — a musical declaration of where Georgia belongs."

Making a Statement Through Campus

Since 2001, the Beethovenfest Bonn has organized the Campus project, a platform for exchange among young musicians, with a focus on countries experiencing historic transformation.

"Previous projects have included Ukraine, Afghanistan, Iran and now, for the second time, Georgia — after first participating in 2003," says Thomas Scheider, who leads the Campus project team at the Beethovenfest. "These are places where culture is not simply a side effect of history, but becomes a central field where history is understood, negotiated and questioned."

For the Federal Youth Orchestra (BJO), which has been a partner in shaping the Campus project for 10 years, the encounter also went far beyond music. "Although music is naturally at the center, the exchange showed so much more: personal connections, cultural richness, significant history, impressive nature and also the challenging current political situation," says Sönke Lentz, orchestra director of the BJO and one of the project organizers. "Pro-European artists and what is likely the vast majority of the population need our solidarity and support."

The Federal Youth Orchestra also incorporated the Campus project into this year's international tour, performing three concerts in Georgia under the direction of Mirian Khukhunaishvili and featuring soloist Giorgi Gigashvili. "Sold-out venues in Tbilisi and Kutaisi, with standing ovations, impressed us and showed us the importance of a project like this," says Sönke Lentz.

Tsotne Zedginidze: Georgian Prodigy and Campus Composer

"The new Mozart" — that is how none other than conductor Daniel Barenboim described Georgian pianist and composer Tsotne Zedginidze when he was just 16 years old.

Zedginidze has just turned 17, making him the project's youngest commissioned composer in the project's history. He composed "Chmebi: Georgian Fantasia" for piano and chamber orchestra. The Georgian word "chmebi" means "voices." The young composer himself will play piano at at the world premiere in Bonn and the subsequent performance in Berlin. "Beethoven would be completely shocked, but it would inspire him," Tsotne says with a smile about his work and the project as a whole.



In his score, Zedginidze draws on ancient, complex Georgian folk traditions for the first time, combining them with unconventional harmonies and fiery folk dance elements. "About my Georgian Fantasia, I tried not to be artificial. It resembles as much as possible Georgian music — all Genres and styles. But at the same time, it's my individual understanding, my own interpretation of Georgian music," he tells DW

Star violinist Lisa Batiashvili is eagerly awaiting the premiere of Tsotne's work. Through her foundation ((name of the foundation?)), the musician, who moved from Georgia to Germany at age 12, supports young artists in her home country. Tsotne is among the foundation's scholarship recipients.

"Over the past 20 years, I have been able to witness how the friendship between Germany and Georgia has grown and how openly and with such interest people here have approached my home country," says Batiashvili. "It is especially beautiful to see young musicians from both countries making music together, learning from each other and inspiring one another." And perhaps, Batiashvili says, something greater than music can emerge from this: a vision of a shared future.

entries.title: El Nino explained: How the weather pattern affects hurricanes and tropical storms
entries.summary: From drought to major floods and extreme heat, El Nino will have a huge impact on the world's weather. In the Atlantic, it could mean a season without hurricanes.
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

How El Nino is shaping tropical storms worldwide

September 23, 2026

From drought to major floods and extreme heat, El Nino will have a huge impact on the world's weather. In the Atlantic, it could mean a season without hurricanes.

In a typical year, storm watchers have logged several hurricanes by late September. At this point in 2005, one of the most active years on record, five major hurricanes had already churned their way through the Atlantic Ocean — including Katrina, one of the most devastating in US history.

But 2026 has been quiet so far. As of September 23, only six tropical storms had formed over the North Atlantic, and none had intensified into hurricanes — a first since satellites began tracking storms in 1966, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the US.

"In the satellite era, we have never had a year without a hurricane," said Matthew Rosencrans, lead hurricane season forecaster with NOAA's Climate Prediction Center. "This would be a first."

That's due, in large part, to the latest iteration of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a shifting cycle of winds and sea surface temperatures over the Pacific Ocean that shapes weather worldwide and makes it a "dominant factor in total hurricane season activity." Meteorologists have said this year's El Nino could be one of the strongest on record.

Hurricane, typhoon, cyclone — what's the difference?

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center, which tracks Atlantic storm data in the US, said the accumulated cyclone energy of this year's tropical storms — a calculation that factors in storm duration and intensity — was at a record low for so late in the season, which typically peaks on September 10.

None of the six tropical storms registered so far have reached a wind speed of at least 119 kilometers per hour (74 miles per hour) — strong enough to be considered a Category 1 hurricane with the potential to cause some minor damage to homes, trees and other infrastructure.

The name for such a catastrophic tropical storm is regional. What's known as a hurricane in the North Atlantic and eastern Pacific will be called a typhoon on the other side of the Pacific, in eastern Asia. In the Indian Ocean and the South Pacific, meteorologists will generally classify a similar storm as a cyclone.

How does El Nino affect Atlantic hurricanes?

NOAA's latest data showed that El Nino is still strengthening, with sea surface temperature rise in the key Pacific region now exceeding 3 degrees Celsius (5.4 Fahrenheit), creating a "very strong" El Nino over the next half year — and a "below-normal" hurricane season.

Almost all Atlantic tropical cyclone activity occurs between June 1 and November 30, though hurricanes can form at other times of the year. And meteorologists have warned that this year's calm doesn't rule out a major hurricane before the season is done.

The naturally occurring El Nino weather pattern returns on average every two to seven years, with its effects lasting up to a year. During El Nino, the regular trade winds moving east-west across the Pacific weaken and sometimes even reverse. The changes in humidity and wind shift the jet stream, the strong winds in the upper atmosphere — and disrupt storm formation in the Atlantic.

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center said any hurricanes that do appear in an El Nino year tend to form along the US East Coast and near the Gulf of Mexico, giving them less time to turn into major hurricanes — but also leaving coastal communities with less time to prepare. That pattern is largely dictated by the steering currents when it forms, which typically last around a week.

"Formations deep in the tropics are hampered due to high wind shear," said Rosencrans — the strong changes in wind speed or direction at different altitudes are more likely to disrupt storm formation. "The stronger the El Nino event, the stronger the wind shear."

Pacific typhoons change track, head north

During El Nino, vertical wind shear isn't as strong in the eastern and central Pacific Ocean. Combined with the warmer waters in the Pacific, which fuel storms with heat and moisture, that tends to result in an increase in tropical cyclones in this region. This part of the Pacific has already seen several major hurricanes this year, including Polo, which this week has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades — fueled in part by El Nino.

"Typically, El Nino means the storms form further east […] toward the international date line and Marshall Islands," Rosencrans told DW, anticipating an "above average" hurricane season in the Pacific. "This does mean that storms have longer life spans before reaching large land masses."

Anne-Claire Fontan at the World Meteorological Organization said during an El Nino event, storms on the Asian side of the vast Pacific tend to track "northward, rather than continue westwards towards East and Southeast Asia."

That meant, according to Rosencrans, that Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan and the Korean Peninsula "can face slightly higher odds of tropical storms and typhoons."

Strong El Nino also disrupts storms in Indian Ocean

A strong El Nino will weaken monsoon winds over the Indian subcontinent, often triggering severe drought. It also generally corresponds with a less active tropical cyclone season in the Indian Ocean, said Fontan, a scientific officer with the WMO's Tropical Cyclone Program.

Much like in the Atlantic, increased wind shear in this region can disrupt or delay the formation of storms, which Fontan said lessened the risks for countries in eastern Africa, like Madagascar and Mozambique.

"In terms of overall tropical cyclone activity in the Southwest Indian Ocean, there is a non-linear, or 'bell-shaped,' relationship with ENSO," said Fontan, highlighting El Nino and its opposite phase. "As ENSO moves towards either of its extremes — a strong El Nino or a strong La Nina — tropical cyclone activity in the basin tends to be below normal."

Are El Nino and climate change linked?

The El Nino-Southern Oscillation is a natural phenomenon, and not caused by climate change. And, as Rosencrans pointed out, "the interplay of El Nino or La Nina and the longer-lived changes is just one piece of what makes hurricane seasons active or inactive."

Among those factors is the dry, dusty air drifting out over the Atlantic from the Sahara Desert, which can also suppress hurricanes.

But Fontan said that the especially strong El Nino effect, combined with the warming effects of climate change from burning fossil fuels, is setting the stage for unprecedented weather extremes in the months ahead.

"El Nino is occurring in a warmer world, and this can amplify some of its impacts, including extreme heat, heavy rainfall and drought," she told DW. Already, some forecasters like the UK's Met Office have said the combined effects of El Nino and climate change could shatter heat records in 2027. A new report from the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab has projected that extreme heat could cause nearly half a million more deaths worldwide during this El Nino period, especially in the Global South.

"We are already seeing the disruption and devastation caused by droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to worsen as El Nino intensifies," said Celeste Saulo, head of WMO, in early September, in a stark warning for governments and humanitarian organizations.

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

entries.title: UNGA: World leaders discuss AI, global conflicts
entries.summary: As the UN General Assembly starts its second day, much attention will turn to the war in Iran, artificial intelligence and climate change. Follow live.
entries.content:
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 23, 2026

As the UN General Assembly starts its second day, much attention will turn to the war in Iran, artificial intelligence and climate change. Follow live.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Artificial intelligence, the Iran war, and climate change set to dominate debate on second day of UN General Assembly
  • Trump was among the first speakers to take the stage and said he had a "big decision" to make on Iran, to either make a deal or "annihilate" the country
  • Gathering of world leaders takes place against a backdrop of global conflicts, environmental crisis and massive technical disruption

Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Brazil, Germany, India and Japan renew calls for Security Council reform

Brazil, Germany, India and Japan renew calls for Security Council reform

The foreign ministers of Brazil, Germany, India and Japan on Wednesday called for the reform of the UN Security Council (UNSC), saying it was more urgent than ever.

"Given the increasingly challenging ‌geopolitical environment, UNSC reform ‌is ​more necessary than ever before," the four foreign ministers said ⁠in ​a joint statement issued after the diplomats met on Tuesday.

The Security Council is a 15-member body with five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the UK and US — known as the P5 and 10 rotating members elected to two-year terms by the General Assembly.

Permanent members enjoy veto powers, which often means the body is kept from carrying out resolutions due to conflicts with the interests of one or more of them.

Skip next section UNGA day 2: AI, Iran war, climate to dominate debate

UNGA day 2: AI, Iran war, climate to dominate debate

Beyond speeches by the presidents of Syria, Iran and Ukraine, artificial intelligence (AI), the US-Israeli war in Iran and the still-pressing issue of climate change are set to dominate the agenda at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Wednesday. 

On day 2 of this 81st UNGA session, tech industry leaders Sam Altman (OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic) and Clement Delangue (Hugging Face) will brief an emergency meeting of the 15-member UN Security Council. Their attendance comes as international concerns — raised from within the industry — prompt debate over slowing AI development before the new technology potentially spins out of control with unknown consequences.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday blasted calls to slow the technology as part of a "globalist scheme," brushing aside warnings that it could wipe out humanity within years if left unchecked.

After Trump used his General Assembly speech on Tuesday to threaten the annihilation of Iran and to drive its people to hell, the Islamic Republic's President Masoud Pezeshkian will directly address world leaders for the first time since the start of the war against Iran in February.

The conflict in Iran has settled into a hot stalemate, directly impacting neighboring states militarily and the entire globe economically.

Iranian and US representatives have met on the sidelines of the General Assembly in New York, but, as has been the case for months, a peace deal remains elusive and the flow of oil through the blockaded Strait of Hormuz stunted.

Russia's more than four-and-a-half-year full-scale assault on Ukraine will also be the topic of diplomatic debate on Wednesday, with a Security Council session scheduled for the morning and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy set to address the General Assembly in the afternoon.

Lastly, climate urgency is on the slate, with outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blasting fossil fuel giants for treating the Earth's atmosphere like an "open sewer" for emissions. 

He further chided "big oil" for its greed as the world grapples with armed conflict.

"Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, five major Western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits," he said, noting that at the same time just $34 billion (€29.8 billion) had been invested in helping developing countries adapt to a warming world.

Skip next section Thanks for reading — we'll be back with more soon

Thanks for reading — we'll be back with more soon

Thanks for following this blog for on the first day of the UN General Assembly debate. We'll restart coverage later on Wednesday for day 2 of the event.

What's expected on Wednesday?

On day 2 of the debate, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to take the stage as his country fends off Russia for another winter. US top diplomat Marco Rubio is also expected to meet his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines on Wednesday.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is slated to speak Wednesday, as the US continues its war with Iran.

The UN Security Council will also hold a meeting on AI. Open AI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei are expected to attend the session.  

Skip next section US top diplomat Rubio to meet Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov on Wednesday

US top diplomat Rubio to meet Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov on Wednesday

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will meet Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York City on Wednesday morning, the US State Department said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with President Donald Trump at the UN headquarters on Tuesday to discuss an end to the 4-year-old war with Russia, including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets. 

Skip next section UK's Andy Burnham: 'Britain is back'

UK's Andy Burnham: 'Britain is back'

In his debut as UK prime minister at the UNGA debate, Andy Burnham declared "Britain is back" 10 years after the country dealt with the turbulence caused by Brexit. 

Burnham said the UK is "restoring our stability" and "building a more dynamic economy" while seeking trade and working together with other countries to tackle shared problems.

However, he said the UK needs to deal with forces of division and instability. He said this begins with Britain boosting its defense expenditures as a NATO member state and strengthening European capabilities.

Another issue Burnham addressed was disinformation being sowed online by Russia-aligned actors.

"Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fear," Burnham said. "They've used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organizations — including universities and the BBC. They've amplified far-right narratives."

The UK prime minister said there is evidence that Russia tried to interfere in the 2019 UK general election. He said the Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion ($1.7 billion, €1.5 billion) annually to sow disinformation.

As a solution, Burnham announced the National Centre for Information Defence to fight disinformation which hurts British interests.

Burnham also addressed the issue of AI, saying global standards are needed because "fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance." Burnham said the UK will work on convincing other countries regarding rules on AI transparency and access to AI models.

Skip next section Japan's mission is to lead efforts towards world without nuclear weapons, Takaichi says

Japan's mission is to lead efforts towards world without nuclear weapons, Takaichi says

Japan's conservative Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said it her country's "mission" to lead efforts towards a "world without nuclear weapons."

She said this is because Japan is the "the only country to have ever suffered atomic bombings during war." The US atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki during World War II in 1945 killed and maimed hundreds of thousands people, with the radiation causing illnesses in survivors in the years after.

Takaichi urged a stronger Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty regime. She also warned that North Korea's nuclear and missile programs along with other activities are a "serious threat to international peace and security."

In regards to technology, Takaichi said Japan intends to host an AI safety summit in the future.

The Japanese prime minister also called for a reform of the UN Security Council by expanding both the number of permanent and non-permanent members.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Mongolia, Vietnam, Dominica among afternoon speakers

IN PICTURES: Mongolia, Vietnam, Dominica among afternoon speakers

Here are some photos of leaders who spoke during this afternoon's session of the UNGA:

Skip next section North Korea's vice foreign minister traveling to UNGA

North Korea's vice foreign minister traveling to UNGA

North Korea's Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs Kim Son Gyong has departed from Pyongyang to attend the UN General Assembly debate in New York City, North Korean state media outlet KCNA reported.

It's unclear whether Kim will meet with officials from the Trump administration.

During his first term, Trump pushed for a deal where North Korea would give up its nuclear ambitions in exchange for sanctions relief.

Trump had met with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Singapore, Hanoi and the Korean Demilitarized Zone in 2018 and 2019 to discuss a possible deal, but ultimately a final agreement never materialized after talks broke down in Sweden in October 2019.

Skip next section Zelenskyy meets Trump, says US and Ukraine want war to end before winter

Zelenskyy meets Trump, says US and Ukraine want war to end before winter

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly debate.

In a post on X, Zelenskyy characterized the meeting with Trump as "positive and productive."

"Both the US and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter. We discussed potential de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy," Zelenskyy said.

"I am grateful that in the meantime our teams keep working on launching Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine. This is what will help proect lives, should Russia spurn the negotiations and keep betting on ballistic missile terror against our people this winter and beyond," the Ukrainian leader added. 

Zelenskyy said he also discussed a winter package of air defense for Ukraine with Trump, among other issues.

The negotiation process between Ukraine and Russia is still stalled, with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner visiting Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month to jumpstart the talks.  It comes as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine will hit its 5-year anniversary in February 2027. 

In comments to journalists after the 40-minute meeting, Zelenskyy said the two leaders discussed an energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy said "we are ready for any kind of format of energy ceasefire" if Russia agrees to "not attack our energy system."

Trump has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. He has, without evidence, blamed the Ukrainian attacks for raising the price of diesel fuel, as the US war with Iran disrupts energy shipments from the Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section Macron calls for open-source AI model not dependent on US, China

Macron calls for open-source AI model not dependent on US, China

Towards the end of his wide-ranging address, French President Emmanuel Macron said there was a need for nations to develop their own artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities so as not to be beholden to the US and China.

"France is proud to have a competitive frontier model" he said, likely referring to Mistral AI.

Macron said likeminded nations such as India, Brazil, Singapore, African nations and the Gulf states should pool not only their financial resources but also their data processing capacity.

"I don't want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers. Rather, we must come together to build an open-source frontier model, a cutting-edge model," he told the UN General Assembly.

"Our investment capabilities must be pooled to build a cutting-edge open-source AI model, which we will share. We should not depend on somebody else," he added.

Skip next section Macron: 'Shame on all of us' of failing to do more for Gaza

Macron: 'Shame on all of us' of failing to do more for Gaza

French President Emmanuel Macron was addressing the General Assembly for the last time, as his term limit approaches and presidential elections beckon early next year. 

He alluded to his previous visit to the event in New York, when a dozen countries including France announced plans to recognize Palestinian statehood. 

"I understand that some of you are very cynical," Macron said, and some people would argue this recognition was only on paper and did not address the reality of the situation.

"But what is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza?" he asked. "Some claim that peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. The scenes, the spectacle, it is shameful. Shame on all of us!"

Macron said that what was needed was respect for the "legitimate rights" of the Palestinian people, arguing that this was a "prerequisite for security" not just for Palestinians but also for Israel.

"But all those who claim that Israel's security requires the violation of the sovereignty of all of its neighboring states are making a very fateful error," Macron said. "They are weakening Israel's security, today, and going forward. They are threatening Israel's security, in fact."

What did Macron suggest regarding Ukraine?

Macron said that France and its allies would continue providing "unstinting support" to Kyiv, but he also floated a suggestion similar to those made by others involved either in the conflict or the efforts to broker a stop to the fighting.

He proposed a "double moratorium," saying that both Ukraine and Russia should commit to stop strikes on each others's energy infrastructure and on grain shipments in the Black Sea.

"Winter is coming," Macron said, explaining, "We'd like to express our support [for] a double moratorium. A moratorium on strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure, that's first. And a Black Sea moratorium which would allow us to release grain shipments."

In times of peace both Russia and Ukraine are prolific agricultural exporters, and use the Black Sea to ship their produce.

Part of supporting Ukraine, Macron said, was working to ensure that "useful negotiations" between the two sides start as quickly as possible. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was attending Tuesday's session; Russia's Vladimir Putin was not expected to travel to New York, or at least he has not done so since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Skip next section Trump tells reporters US and Iranian officials met

Trump tells reporters US and Iranian officials met

A few hours after his speech at the assembly warning he was prepared to "annihilate" Iran if necessary, US President Donald Trump told reporters that American and Iranian officials had met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. 

"The had a very good meeting, a very productive meeting," Trump told reporters, saying it had lasted roughly three hours.

"They have another one scheduled in the very near future," he said.

Trump's speech, not unusually for the US president, contained mixed messages on Iran: a combination both of bombastic threats but also assertions that a "deal" to end the fighting was also a realistic prospect.

"I have a big decision to make,” Trump had said during his speech earlier. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

Skip next section Finland's Stubb: Choose cooperation, and competition, over conflict

Finland's Stubb: Choose cooperation, and competition, over conflict

Finland's President Alexander Stubb told the audience that the world faced a "choice between cooperation and conflict." 

He said that a third "c" was natural and should not cause concern, provided the right balance was struck.

"Competition will always be there. Nations compete now harder than they did a generation ago. This doesn't worry me. What does, is that more and more of them now compete against the rules on which the international order rests," Stubb said.

Stubb said he wanted to defend those rules and the spirit of cooperation and multilateralism underpinning them.

"Small nations need it to survive, and large nations need it to be great," said Stubb, president of a country with a population only around the size of the US state of South Carolina or the Chinese city of Jinan.

Stubb said the rules were the best ways to ensure "that competition does not escalate into conflict, and that cooperation gains ground."

Stubb cited a quote, that itself seemed a riff on another Winston Churchill adage, that's sometimes attributed to former US Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott: "Multilateralism is hell and can be a real pain in the neck, but it is the best option for humanity as a whole."

The Finnish president said that "currently, however, we appear to be going the other way — more towards a non-cooperative and multi-polar world order."

Though he said he see it might be tempting, particularly for larger powers, he called it a fundamentally "short-sighted approach" that "will turn against us, whether you represent a great power, a middle power, or a small state like Finland."

Skip next section Lithuania's President Nauseda urges assembly not to forget Ukraine

Lithuania's President Nauseda urges assembly not to forget Ukraine

The first Baltic leader to speak, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, began by delineating his country's plans to help defusing mines in the Strait of Hormuz or helping bring about the Gaza peace plan — but he urged the assembly not to forget the longer-running conflict closest to his home. 

"Ladies and gentleman, the one conflict that poses the greatest threat to the world order is Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine," Nauseda said, even 12 years after it began with the annexation of Crimea and the beginnings of a Russian-backed uprising in eastern Ukraine.

In that time, Nauseda said, "Russia has escalated from clandestine operations and limited warfare in eastern Ukraine to massive military operations, mass killings, and ultimately the largest drone attacks against civilian infrastructure the world has ever seen."

He noted how the full-blown war, starting with Russia's February 2022 invasion, had now lasted longer than the first World War. Nauseda said that despite massive casualties, Russian progress had slowed to a snail's pace and Ukraine's culture, language and institutions stood tall.

Nauseda said that only a Ukrainian victory could safeguard ideals like the UN Charter.

"What we cannot allow is brute force prevailing over international law," he said. "We cannot tolerate any longer Moscow's colonial aspirations."

He said these aspirations reached far into "Europe, Africa and Asia," and said that no country should consider itself immune.

In Lithuania's case, he said Russia's war of aggression had led to "numerous violations of our airspace by combat drones," to intensified hybrid attacks, disinformation and sabotage efforts. 

He said that where Russia advanced in opening this "new Pandora's box of new techniques for destablization, other hostile actors follow, learning new skills and ideas."

Skip next section Qatar's emir says Gulf going through 'one of its most dangerous phases'

Qatar's emir says Gulf going through 'one of its most dangerous phases'

Qatar's Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said the current crisis in the Gulf "should come as no surprise to anyone" as he took to the podium in New York. 

"It is the cumulative result of years of postponing crisis management through temporary solutions and unrealistic policies," he said of the war between the US and Iran which has sprawled to impact a series of Gulf states. 

"At the heart of the dangerous situation we are witnessing lies an absence of a regional system of collective security," Al Thani said. "One that respects the sovereignty, security and territorial integrity of states. One that promotes the peaceful settlement of disputes and the non-interference in the internal affairs of states."

He said Qatar had recently called "from this very podium" for such a system and was now reiterating the appeal "after recent events have demonstrated the urgent need for it."

The emir said, without naming Iran or the US at any point in his address, that the absence of such a regional accord had allowed "one party to drag its neighbors into a war that is not theirs, targeting their vital assets and installations, despite their strenuous efforts to avert escalation."

Iran has sometimes struck targets in neighboring Gulf countries with close ties to the US.

Al Thani said that the restrictions on passage through the Strait of Hormuz amounted to the "lifelines of the global economy" being turned into bargaining chips, "with people on every continent bearing the cost, despite being far removed from the causes of the conflict."

The 46-year-old head of state said this was driving up prices not just for fuel but also for core other goods like food and medicine.

entries.title: China's new travel rules unsettle tech giants and talent
entries.summary: Beijing is locking the gates to stop expertise and capital in strategic industries from fleeing. The country accused of industrial-scale intellectual property theft now fears the West will take its own.
entries.content:
September 23, 2026

Beijing is locking the gates to stop expertise and capital in strategic industries from fleeing. The country accused of industrial-scale intellectual property theft now fears the West will take its own.

For decades, China has faced accusations from the United States and the European Union of stealing their technology.

From robotics and advanced semiconductors to precision engineering and automotive parts, Chinese firms have recruited top engineers, allegedly spied on Western rivals and been linked to cyberattacks aimed at gaining access to valuable trade secrets.

It is perhaps ironic, then, that China is now taking steps to prevent its own high-end technologies and talent from escaping abroad.

China's Great Wall around its top brains

Last week, new entry-exit rules took effect, giving Chinese authorities the power to stop engineers, founders and other specialists from leaving the country if their expertise in batteries, rare earths or artificial intelligence (AI) is judged a threat to "industrial and technological security."

Recently, China has also tightened outbound-investment rules, cracked down on Chinese nationals holding their wealth offshore and restricted the posting of technical staff overseas.

Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University (SMU), believes that, taken together, the curbs "offer a rare glimpse into the true state of China's economy."

"These measures suggest that Beijing is deeply concerned about economic weakness and substantial capital outflows," Gao told DW, adding that authorities are also determined to stop "entrepreneurs and skilled personnel from leaving the country."

The strain on China's economy is increasingly hard to hide. While demand for exports remains strong — especially for high-tech goods — the country's property crash has severely weakened domestic consumption.

Bank lending fell to a record low over the summer, and new car sales in August dropped nearly a quarter year-on-year.

Beijing blocks deals, founders seek exit

The same anxiety now extends to people and money leaving. The most prominent recent example is Manus, an AI startup created by two Chinese nationals in Beijing. Last year, the company moved its headquarters to Singapore, partly to avoid US investment curbs and expand into global markets.

When Facebook owner Meta tried to acquire Manus last December for $2 billion (€1.74 billion), Beijing blocked the move and barred the firm's two founders from leaving the country.

Just this month, Chinese social media has been awash with rumors that Huawei founder and CEO Ren Zhengfei and his daughter, CFO Meng Wanzhou, may have left the country.

The claims were picked up by Taiwanese and Indian media outlets but have not been confirmed by the tech giant and Chinese authorities. At least one family member has since appeared in public in Beijing.

Wealthy Chinese struggle to get capital out

Bloomberg Intelligence estimated that some $1 trillion in Chinese wealth had exited the country last year — the largest amount of "hot money" leaving since 2006, when records began.

Beijing has not tightened its annual $50,000 foreign-exchange quota that households may take out of the country. What has tightened, says Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at French investment bank Natixis, are the unofficial routes the wealthy used around that cap.

"They haven't changed the $50,000 quota. They are now squeezing the people and agents that money usually travels with," Garcia-Herrero told DW.

An entire industry has grown up, in China and abroad, to help people get themselves and their capital out. Emigration agents arrange visas and relocations, while offshore brokers and trusts help Chinese nationals to park wealth overseas.

Companies sometimes use a foreign subsidiary, a listing or a staff posting to take money and know-how out together.

New rules may spur workarounds

SMU's Gao believes the new curbs may prove counterproductive, as the more difficult it becomes to move capital or people abroad, the greater the incentive for those with the means to find other ways out.

"Over time, that could further erode confidence, accelerate capital flight and deepen the very economic problems the measures are intended to contain," Gao told DW.

Garcia-Herrero, meanwhile, thinks the block on talent will matter more than the squeeze on capital.

"You can still move money slowly, with approvals," she told DW. "You cannot easily replace a process engineer who cannot board a plane — or who will not take an overseas job because of an indefinite ban."

AI talent now needs permission to fly

The risk is already hitting China's AI firms, which are fast catching up with their US rivals in the race to produce the most advanced AI systems.

In May, Bloomberg reported that Chinese authorities now required top AI researchers, founders and executives at firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to obtain approval before traveling abroad.

Last year, some DeepSeek staff were asked to hand in their passports, according to tech news site The Information. Beijing has neither confirmed nor denied the practice.

Bloomberg reported in January last year that other tech engineers face similar pressure, including those helping foreign firms cut their reliance on China by building factories in Vietnam and India.

Lawyers and officials tighten legal advice

For foreign nationals, both Chinese and foreign firms sometimes disguise a working visit to China to avoid scrutiny and visa delays. They may suggest a trip is for tourism, business meetings or a factory tour rather than actual work.

Ahead of the new curbs, international law firms like DLA Piper advised companies to keep visa filings "truthful" and "complete," warning that a mismatch between the paperwork and the actual work could now mean an entry ban of up to five years.

The new rules state that a visitor should, in principle, be told if they are banned. However, Chinese authorities may withhold notification if it "may affect national security or the investigation of criminal cases."

In an updated travel advisory earlier this month, the US State Department went further, warning Americans to "exercise increased caution in mainland China due to ... the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Famine threatens the Ukrainian town of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region as Russia delays creating a humanitarian evacuation corridor
entries.summary: Food supplies to the town of Oleshky in the occupied part of the southern Kherson region have been cut off since May. Efforts by Kyiv to negotiate the evacuation of civilians with Moscow have been largely unsuccessful.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Warnings of famine grow in Ukrainian town of Oleshky

September 23, 2026

Food supplies to the town of Oleshky in the occupied part of the southern Kherson region have been cut off since May. Efforts by Kyiv to negotiate the evacuation of civilians with Moscow have been largely unsuccessful.

A man sends a photo of "Oleshky borsch," a vegetable soup he has made from leftovers. To make the soup more filling, he says he has added millet and two eggs.

"Today, we have a delicacy in our borsch. My mother traded 2.5 kilograms (5.5 pounds) of sugar for 10 eggs," he tells the recipient of the photo, Tetiana Hasanenko, the head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, which is based in territory controlled by Kyiv. "There's no cabbage in it, but there is asparagus," he adds.

Hasanenko says she's used to getting such messages. "I receive reports like this every day," Hasanenko told DW. "People want to be given some kind of hope, but there is no hope." She said food was last delivered to the town at the end of May. "The situation is critical," she said, warning that "you can't just call this starvation — it's a famine."

Oleshky is located in Ukraine'ssouthern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River. The city has been occupied since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.Russia's full-scale invasionin February 2022. 

In June 2023, the town was almost completely flooded after a blast at the Kakhovka Power Plant and the breach of the Kakhovka Dam.

Hasanenko said the situation worsened last winter. She said there were about 6,000 people left in the area, including 180 children. They have already become accustomed to living without electricity and gas and have to fetch water from wells. Now, they have to prepare for another harsh winter.



'One kilo of zucchini for 1,000 rubles'

"To be honest, I haven't eaten anything yet," resident Halyna (whose name has been changed for security reasons) told DW by phone at around lunchtime. "My best option for today is a flatbread made of water and flour, as there's still some left. I spread apple sauce on it and make myself some tea without sugar. That's about it."

People only go out between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m., she explained, adding that they tended to gather in the market square to hear the latest news and would trade or sell food from their supplies or gardens.

"Today, there were a few zucchinis for 1,000 rubles (€10 or $11.4) per kilo," she said, adding that someone had sold a large sack of flour for 200,000 rubles. She speculated that he was probably going to try to leave Oleshky, which is why the price was so high.

Minibuses used to run from Oleshky to Skadovsk about an hour south and then to Crimea or Russia. They also transported food to Oleshky for sale. After they were attacked by drones, two ambulances were deployed instead. "But for the past month and a half, none of the ambulances have been running, because one of the drivers was killed on a trip," Halyna reported.

She explained that people are now stocking up on food in the village of Radensk, located 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) to the south. People walk there or ride their bikes.

Anyone who wants to be evacuated must reach the village of Tarasivka, which is another 20 kilometers away. From there, you can get to Skadovsk by minibus or by hitchhiking. However, the route is heavily mined. "You set out and could die along the way," Halyna said, adding that two women who were trying to get food died that way.

According to Halyna, scores of people in Oleshky have been injured by mines and explosive devices. But they can't count on medical help.

"If your leg is blown off, you're as good as dead. There's a surgeon at the hospital, but no anesthesiologist and no medicine," she said. Conditions are also deteriorating for inpatients. "Last winter, they still got some soup and two pieces of baked dough," she said, adding that now there's one and a half spoonfuls of semolina porridge cooked in water and cold tea.

Moreover, evacuating from Oleshky is difficult not only because of the danger of landmines. Many residents have neither a Russian nor a Ukrainian passport. In addition, people lack cash.

Moscow lacks evacuation willingness

"There is only one solution: A 'green corridor' must be established and the people evacuated. The occupying authorities must move the people deeper into the temporarily occupied territory," says Tetiana Hasanenko of the Ukrainian military administration.

Talks about an evacuation from Oleshky have been ongoing since last spring. At that time, at the initiative of the Ukrainian parliamentary human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, city officials compiled a list of residents who wish to leave the municipality of Oleshky.

"358 people need to be evacuated urgently," he wrote on social media. "These are only the ones we've heard about," he emphasized, noting that the town of Oleshky currently has more than 6,000 residents. "These people must be rescued because the town has become a death trap," the ombudsman said.

According to him, preliminary agreements had been reached between Kyiv and Moscow. The Ukrainian military was to ensure a ceasefire, and the International Committee of the Red Cross was to assist with the evacuation. But Russia "has not reaffirmed its willingness" to carry out the evacuation "for quite some time," Lubinets said.

Meanwhile, the residents of Oleshky are desperate, says Tetiana Hasanenko. "They had hoped that the evacuation would begin at any moment. But what now? I can't give them any hope at all," she laments.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

entries.title: World lagging on key UN biodiversity targets
entries.summary: Hundreds of nations signed on to a goal to protect 30% of the world's land and sea by 2030. As the timeline reaches the halfway point, activists say the current protection estimates are way behind.
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

World lagging on key UN biodiversity targets

September 23, 2026

Hundreds of nations signed on to a goal to protect 30% of the world's land and sea by 2030. As the timeline reaches the halfway point, activists say the current protection estimates are way behind.

World governments are off track to meet a historic United Nations target to protect at least 30% of the planet's land and seas by the year 2030, according to a new study published Wednesday.

The research by environmental groups Campaign for Nature and Together for the Ocean shows that about 20% of land and inland waters are designated as protected or conserved, following the signing of the 30×30 goal in 2022.

If nations fully deliver on existing quantified commitments, the estimate could increase to 27% by the turn of the decade, the report said.

The 30x30 goal was adopted under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework at COP15 and was signed by nearly 200 nations that pledged at least $200 billion (about €175 billion) annually to reduce biodiversity loss.

Only 'a third' of target reached in ocean protection

For the world's oceans, the study says protection is "lagging."

The coverage is currently at 10% of global ocean and could only reach 12% by 2030, the research revealed.

"The ocean is emerging as one of the defining implementation challenges of 30×30," Together for the Ocean said, adding that important marine ecosystems, like offshore and deep-sea habitats, remain "vulnerable."

Last month, the Convention on Biological Diversity, the UN treaty dedicated to the global nature goals, also cautioned that countries were not on track.

Funding gap

The report singled out finance for conservation as "one of the greatest barriers" to reaching global targets.

The research said that between $100 billion and $180 billion was needed each year to make the 2030 target. Current annual spending, however, amounted to just $24 billion.

"The gap is particularly stark for the ocean, where approximately $16 billion is needed annually, but only an estimated $ 1.8 billion is currently spent," the study said.

From October 19, the UN biodiversity summit in Yerevan will see the nations address the progress shortfall and assess ways of getting back on target.

Edited by: Sean Sinco

entries.title: Germany news: Call to scrap once-a-day gas price rises
entries.summary: The ADAC motoring association says a once-a-day rule on gas price changes has failed to help drivers' wallets. Entry-level jobs are becoming scarcer, making things hard for those entering the job market. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Call to scrap once-a-day gas price rises

Published September 23, 2026last updated September 23, 2026

The ADAC motoring association says a once-a-day rule on gas price changes has failed to help drivers' wallets. Entry-level jobs are becoming scarcer, making things hard for those entering the job market. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A rule allowing gas stations to raise prices only at noon has not achieved its objective of lowering them, motoring association ADAC says
  • The number of entry-level jobs has dropped by two-thirds since 2022, an online job exchange says
  • Traces of explosives have been found near a German military base close to where drone parts were discovered last week, security sources say

Here is a roundup of headline stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, September 23, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereClick here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Suspected explosives traces discovered close to drone find near Bundeswehr air base

Suspected explosives traces discovered close to drone find near Bundeswehr air base

Investigators have found suspected traces of explosives near the Bundeswehr air base in Wunstorf, Lower Saxony, after drone parts were found in the area.

German media report that the investigators believe the drone could have been equipped with explosives, as the suspicious substances were found just meters away from it.

However, the reports said examinations of the traces had not yet been concluded.

The drone parts in Wunstorf were found by chance, and the media reports said they may have been lying there for two years.

It remains unknown where the drone came from, but security sources say it had construction similarities with an explosives-laden drone found at the Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August.

The German government has accused Russia of being behind the incident at the airport as an attempted attack on Ukrainian cargo planes there.

The air base near Wunstorf is an important military site that is home to Germany's fleet of A400M transport planes.

Skip next section Activists climb on CDU headquarters in Berlin to protest climate policies

Activists climb on CDU headquarters in Berlin to protest climate policies

Activists from the Robin Wood group have rappelled down the facade of the Konrad-Adenauer-Haus in Berlin — the headquarters of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU)  — in a protest against climate inaction and call for more resistance to right-wing extremism.

The activists attached a large red banner to the building calling on the conservative-led government to "end welfare cuts [and] fight [the] climate crisis," and to take a firm stance against the far right.

The banner covered a picture of the CDU's top candidate at recent state elections in Berlin, Stefan Evers, who is currently finance senator (minister) in the city-state.

A statement handed out at the location stated: "We protest against the policies of the CDU-led federal government, which is dropping climate protection and has no concepts on how to stop the rise of the right-wing extremist AfD."

Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reicheof the CDU in particular has come under fire from several quarters for policies that many see as putting the brakes on Germany's transition to renewable sources.

The conservative CDU/CSU parliamentary bloc has also been criticized for adopting some of the harsh anti-migration measures advocated by the AfD in a seeming bid to win back voters from the far-right party.

Skip next section Entry-level jobs in Germany see sharp decline — online job exchange

Entry-level jobs in Germany see sharp decline — online job exchange

Offers for entry-level jobs have dropped by two-thirds since 2022, when they were at a record high, according to an analysis by the online job exchange Indeed.

The drop is considerably larger than that of jobs overall, which fell by 39% in that time, Indeed said.

The decline in entry-level jobs since 2022 is across almost all sectors, Indeed said, with a drop in offers in 26 of the 28 employment types examined.

In 23 of these, the fall was greater than in the overall labor market.

Knowledge professions and office jobs were the hardest-hit, with 75% fewer entry-level job offers in the marketing sector, 77% fewer in the field of IT applications and solutions and 60% fewer in the project management area.

Just two sectors showed a rise, according to the analysis: care professions, medicine and pharmacy (18% more) and food, gastronomy and the hotel industry (10% more).

Indeed economist Virginia Sondergeld said young people faced a rising risk of beginning their careers with a phase of unemployment.

But she said there was so far no evidence that the rise of artificial intelligence, which many see as threatening human employment, affected job chances, attributing the drop rather to the current economic downturn.

"People entering the jobs market are the first victims of the weak economy, as companies first of all save money where they should be investing in young workers," she said.

Skip next section 248 people drown during German summer

248 people drown during German summer

Between May and mid-September, 248 people died in drowning accidents in Germany, 12 more than in the same period last year, the German Life Saving Association (DLRG) said on Wednesday.

June, which saw a prolonged heat wave, was the month with the most drownings: 101 people lost their lives in the water, the highest number since 2003.

However, the number of drowning deaths this year, 320, is slightly under that of last year (328), according to the DLRG.

The DLRG said that the number of young drowning victims was notable, with 88 people between the ages of 11 and 30 drowning since the start of the year — 15 more than in the whole of 2025.

More than 90% of the victims in this age group were male.

The DLRG said young men tend to be less cautious and more prone to overestimating themselves, while many lack swimming skills.

It called for more education about dangers and better swimming instruction, particularly at schools.

Skip next section ADAC calls to drop once-a-day price rise rule for fuel

ADAC calls to drop once-a-day price rise rule for fuel

The ADAC motoring association has said that a rule in force since April 1 allowing gas stations to raise fuel prices only once a day, at noon, has not brought down prices and "should therefore be abolished."

Although the rule had greatly reduced the number of price changes throughout a day and made increases easier to predict, the gap between the highest and lowest prices had increased, the ADAC said.

It also said motorists who needed to buy gas shortly after noon, when gas stations have typically jacked up prices, were faced with unjustifiably higher costs.

An economic research institute, ZEW, also found in April that prices were higher on average after the rule was introduced, with fuel prices generally going up after noon and cheaper in the morning.

Fuel prices in Germany and Europe in general have skyrocketed amid the war in the Middle East.

The ADAC reported that average gas prices in Germany hit a record high on Thursday, reaching €2.308 for a liter of super E10 and €2.471 for a liter of diesel ($9.98/US gallon and $10.69/US gallon, respectively)

In its statement, the ADAC, however, welcomed the government's temporary reduction in the energy tax that is planned to go into force on October 1, saying it was the most realistic way to lower the burden on motorists.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn wishes all users of Germany's international broadcaster guten Tag!

The high gas prices largely caused by fallout from the Iran war continue to be a major topic in Germany, with the country's main motoring association, the ADAC, now saying one government measure introduced in April in a bid to reduce the burden on motorists has failed.

And a lifesaving association has sad news after the unusually warm summer, with more drowning deaths from May to mid-September in Germany than in the same period last year.

Read on to find out more about these and other stories.
